warmup.q: The card issuer allows 20 concurrent calls from your service. You move a 10,000-payment batch to virtual threads. What is the right way to stay under the issuer's limit?
options: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()): a pool of 20 virtual threads
Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), and one shared Semaphore(20) acquired around the issuer call
Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() on its own, since virtual threads limit themselves to the core count
A new Semaphore(20) inside each payment's task
warmup.why: Limit the resource, not the threads. A pool of 20 also limits everything else each task does, so work that needs no limit waits too. The per-task executor has no limit at all: it will start 10,000 virtual threads. A semaphore created per task gives every task its own 20 permits, which limits nothing. One shared semaphore around the call is the only option that caps the issuer at 20.

sections.h: Five ways to start a virtual thread
sections.html:
JDK 21 has no new VirtualThread(). You start virtual threads through the Thread.Builder API or through an executor:

Java
// 1. a one-off, no name
Thread a = Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> settle(p));

// 2. a builder, when you want a name in thread dumps
Thread b = Thread.ofVirtual().name("auth-", 0).start(() -> settle(p));   // auth-0

// 3. created now, started later
Thread c = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(() -> settle(p));
c.start();

// 4. a ThreadFactory, for libraries and frameworks that take one
ThreadFactory vtf = Thread.ofVirtual().name("ledger-", 0).factory();
ExecutorService named = Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(vtf);

// 5. what you'll use most: one new virtual thread per task
ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
Kotlin
// 1. a one-off, no name
val a = Thread.startVirtualThread { settle(p) }

// 2. a builder, when you want a name in thread dumps
val b = Thread.ofVirtual().name("auth-", 0).start { settle(p) }   // auth-0

// 3. created now, started later
val c = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted { settle(p) }
c.start()

// 4. a ThreadFactory, for libraries and frameworks that take one
val vtf = Thread.ofVirtual().name("ledger-", 0).factory()
val named = Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(vtf)

// 5. what you'll use most: one new virtual thread per task
val perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()

The builder with name("auth-", 0) numbers its threads: the first is auth-0, the next auth-1. A builder object is not thread safe, so build it in one place. The factory it returns is thread safe, so share that.

Use the executor in normal code. It gives you Futures, it has a close() that waits, and every framework already knows how to take an ExecutorService. Use the builder when you start a single long-lived thread, such as a Kafka poll loop, and want a name you can find in a thread dump. Virtual threads have no name by default, which makes a dump of 50,000 of them hard to read.

All of these return ordinary Thread objects. join, interrupt and isAlive work as usual, and isVirtual() tells you which kind you have.

try.title: Start one of each
steps: Run BuildersDemo. Each line is printed from inside the new thread.
Predict before you look: which ones have a name, and what is isDaemon() for each?
Add .daemon(false) before .start(...) on the ofVirtual() line (in either file) and run again. What happens?

code.title: BuildersDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadFactory; /** Every way to start a virtual thread in JDK 21+, with what each one prints. */ public class BuildersDemo { static void show(String how) { Thread t = Thread.currentThread(); System.out.printf("%-34s name=%-10s virtual=%-5s daemon=%s%n", how, "'" + t.getName() + "'", t.isVirtual(), t.isDaemon()); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // 1. the shortcut: start one now, no name Thread a = Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> show("Thread.startVirtualThread")); a.join(); // 2. the builder: name it, then start it Thread b = Thread.ofVirtual().name("auth-7").start(() -> show("Thread.ofVirtual().name().start")); b.join(); // 3. unstarted: create now, start later Thread c = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(() -> show("Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted")); c.start(); c.join(); // 4. a factory with numbered names, for code that wants a ThreadFactory ThreadFactory factory = Thread.ofVirtual().name("ledger-", 0).factory(); try (ExecutorService named = Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(factory)) { for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) named.submit(() -> show("newThreadPerTaskExecutor(factory)")); } // 5. the one you'll use most: a new virtual thread per task, closed with try-with-resources try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<String> f = perTask.submit(() -> { show("newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor"); return "approved"; }); System.out.println("future result: " + f.get()); } // close() waits for every task submitted above } }

alt.title: BuildersDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.vthreads.l03 import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** Every way to start a virtual thread in JDK 21+, called from Kotlin, with what each one prints. */ private fun show(how: String) { val t = Thread.currentThread() println("%-34s name=%-10s virtual=%-5s daemon=%s".format(how, "'${t.name}'", t.isVirtual, t.isDaemon)) } fun main() { // 1. the shortcut: start one now, no name Thread.startVirtualThread { show("Thread.startVirtualThread") }.join() // 2. the builder: name it, then start it Thread.ofVirtual().name("auth-7").start { show("Thread.ofVirtual().name().start") }.join() // 3. unstarted: create now, start later val c = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted { show("Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted") } c.start() c.join() // 4. a factory with numbered names, for code that wants a ThreadFactory val factory = Thread.ofVirtual().name("ledger-", 0).factory() Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(factory).use { named -> repeat(2) { named.submit { show("newThreadPerTaskExecutor(factory)") } } } // 5. the one you'll use most: a new virtual thread per task, closed with use {} Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> val f = perTask.submit(Callable { show("newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor") "approved" }) println("future result: ${f.get()}") } // close() waits for every task submitted above }

try.expect: Only auth-7, ledger-0 and ledger-1 have names; the rest print an empty name. Every line says virtual=true daemon=true. The .daemon(false) edit doesn't compile, in Java or in Kotlin: Thread.ofVirtual() returns a Thread.Builder.OfVirtual, which has no daemon method, because virtual threads are always daemon threads.

sections.h: One task, one virtual thread, one try block
sections.html:
newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() starts a brand-new virtual thread for every task you submit. It keeps no threads around and has no queue. Its Javadoc says it plainly: the number of threads it creates is unbounded.

Since JDK 19, ExecutorService is AutoCloseable. close() shuts the executor down and then waits until every submitted task has finished. So the shape of a fan-out is one try-with-resources block:

Java
List<Receipt> authorizeAll(List<Payment> batch) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
    try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        // 1. fork: start every call before waiting for any
        List<Future<Receipt>> futures = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Payment p : batch) futures.add(perTask.submit(() -> issuer.authorize(p)));
        // 2. join: collect in input order
        List<Receipt> receipts = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Future<Receipt> f : futures) receipts.add(f.get());
        return receipts;
    }   // 3. close(): waits for any task still running
}
Kotlin
fun authorizeAll(batch: List<Payment>): List<Receipt> =
    Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask ->
        // 1. fork: start every call before waiting for any
        val futures = batch.map { p -> perTask.submit(Callable { issuer.authorize(p) }) }
        // 2. join: collect in input order
        futures.map { it.get() }
    }   // 3. close(): waits for any task still running

Create the executor where the work starts, and let it end where the work ends. A short-lived executor per request or per batch costs almost nothing, because it doesn't own any threads. It also means that when this method returns, no thread it started is still running. That property gets a name and a whole API in lesson 5 of this track.

In a Kafka consumer the natural unit is the poll batch: one executor block per batch, one virtual thread per record, and the offset commit after the block closes, when every record has finished. Do this only for topics where records with the same key don't have to be processed in order, because the virtual threads finish in any order.

Two details trip people up. Start every task before you call get() on any of them. A loop that submits one task and then waits on it runs your batch one call at a time, on 5,000 threads. And get() reports a failed task as an ExecutionException whose cause is the real exception. The other tasks keep running when one fails, and close() still waits for them. Cancelling them is also lesson 5's topic.

This executor has no limit, and that is deliberate. A limit belongs somewhere else, which the next two sections show.

Check yourself: a teammate submits each payment and calls get() on its future before submitting the next. With 5,000 payments and a 120 ms issuer, how long does the batch take, and how many calls are in flight at once? About 10 minutes (5,000 × 0.12 s), with one call in flight. That is Little's law with L = 1, and 5,000 virtual threads didn't help at all.

Thread pools exist for two reasons: platform threads are expensive to create, so you reuse them, and a fixed pool caps how much work runs at once. Neither reason survives virtual threads.

Creating a virtual thread costs about as much as creating a small object, so reuse saves almost nothing. And a pool is the wrong place for a cap, because it caps everything the task does, not just the one call that needs it.

Here is the mistake, in code that compiles and runs fine:

Java
// anti-pattern: a pool of 20 virtual threads to protect a 20-connection database
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofVirtual().factory());
pool.execute(() -> {
    Risk risk = fraud.check(p);      // 60 ms, needs no limit, but waits for a pool slot anyway
    ledger.record(p, risk);          // 10 ms, the only call that needs the limit
});
Kotlin
// anti-pattern: a pool of 20 virtual threads to protect a 20-connection database
val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofVirtual().factory())
pool.execute {
    val risk = fraud.check(p)        // 60 ms, needs no limit, but waits for a pool slot anyway
    ledger.record(p, risk)           // 10 ms, the only call that needs the limit
}

Each task holds a pool slot for 70 ms, so 1,000 payments take 1,000 / 20 × 70 ms = 3.5 s. If only the ledger call is limited, the fraud calls all overlap. The batch then takes about 60 ms plus 1,000 / 20 × 10 ms, about 0.56 s. Same database limit, six times faster.

Pooled threads bring a second problem with them: ThreadLocals survive from one task to the next on a reused thread. Lesson 4 of this track covers that.

The rule from JEP 444 is short. Never pool virtual threads. Create one per task, and put the limit on the resource.

Pools are still the right tool for platform threads doing CPU work. A newFixedThreadPool(cores) for hashing, PDF rendering or signature checks keeps that work bounded and off the virtual thread scheduler. The rule is about virtual threads only.

try.title: A pool vs a semaphore, same limit
steps: Read PoolVsSemaphoreDemo. Each request makes a 60 ms fraud call and a 10 ms ledger call, and the ledger allows 20 at once.
Predict both times with the arithmetic above, then run it.
Change DB_LIMIT to 50 and predict again. Which version speeds up more?

code.title: PoolVsSemaphoreDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; /** * Each request calls the fraud service (60 ms, no limit) and then the ledger database * (10 ms, at most 20 at once). Two ways to respect the database limit: * a pool of 20 virtual threads, or one virtual thread per request plus a Semaphore(20). */ public class PoolVsSemaphoreDemo { static final int REQUESTS = 1_000; static final int DB_LIMIT = 20; static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { // A: the anti-pattern. The pool size limits the database, and also everything else. long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(DB_LIMIT, Thread.ofVirtual().factory())) { for (int i = 0; i < REQUESTS; i++) { pool.execute(() -> { sleep(60); // fraud check: needs no limit sleep(10); // ledger write: needs the limit }); } } System.out.printf("pool of %d virtual threads: %,5d ms%n", DB_LIMIT, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); // B: one virtual thread per request; the semaphore guards only the database call Semaphore db = new Semaphore(DB_LIMIT); long t1 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < REQUESTS; i++) { perTask.execute(() -> { sleep(60); // all 1,000 fraud checks overlap try { db.acquire(); // at most 20 inside the database } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; } try { sleep(10); } finally { db.release(); } }); } } System.out.printf("virtual thread per task + Semaphore(%d): %,5d ms%n", DB_LIMIT, (System.nanoTime() - t1) / 1_000_000); } }

Two ways to respect the database limit: * a pool of 20 virtual threads, or one virtual thread per request plus a Semaphore(20). */ private const val REQUESTS = 1_000 private const val DB_LIMIT = 20 fun main() { // A: the anti-pattern. The pool size limits the database, and also everything else. val t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(DB_LIMIT, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()).use { pool -> repeat(REQUESTS) { pool.execute { Thread.sleep(60) // fraud check: needs no limit Thread.sleep(10) // ledger write: needs the limit } } } println("pool of %d virtual threads: %,5d ms".format(DB_LIMIT, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) // B: one virtual thread per request; the semaphore guards only the database call val db = Semaphore(DB_LIMIT) val t1 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> repeat(REQUESTS) { perTask.execute { Thread.sleep(60) // all 1,000 fraud checks overlap db.acquire() // at most 20 inside the database try { Thread.sleep(10) } finally { db.release() } } } } println("virtual thread per task + Semaphore(%d): %,5d ms".format(DB_LIMIT, (System.nanoTime() - t1) / 1_000_000)) }

try.expect: The pool takes about 3.5 s (one run here: 3,584 ms) and the semaphore version about 0.6 s (586 ms). With a limit of 50 the pool drops to about 1.4 s and the semaphore version to about 0.26 s. Both respect the database limit; only the pool also slows down the work that has no limit.

sections.h: Limit the resource with a shared Semaphore
sections.html:
A Semaphore holds a number of permits. acquire() takes one, and waits if none are left. release() gives one back and wakes a waiter. On a virtual thread, waiting in acquire() parks the thread, so 5,000 waiters cost 5,000 small heap objects and no OS threads.

The pattern has three rules:

Java
final class IssuerClient {
    private final Semaphore inFlight = new Semaphore(20);   // 1. one per resource, shared by all callers
    private final IssuerHttp http;

    IssuerClient(IssuerHttp http) { this.http = http; }

    Auth authorize(Payment p) throws InterruptedException {
        inFlight.acquire();                               // 2. acquire outside the try
        try {
            return http.authorize(p);                     // only the call that needs the limit
        } finally {
            inFlight.release();                           // 3. always give it back
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
class IssuerClient(private val http: IssuerHttp) {
    private val inFlight = Semaphore(20)                 // 1. one per resource, shared by all callers

    fun authorize(p: Payment): Auth {
        inFlight.acquire()                               // 2. acquire outside the try
        try {
            return http.authorize(p)                     // only the call that needs the limit
        } finally {
            inFlight.release()                           // 3. always give it back
        }
    }
}

The semaphore lives with the resource, as a field on the client that every request uses. A semaphore created inside a request handler gives each request its own 20 permits and limits nothing. acquire() sits before the try, so a thread interrupted while waiting never releases a permit it didn't get. If it did, the limit would quietly grow to 21, then 22.

Pick the number from the downstream side: the issuer's documented concurrency limit, or the size of the database connection pool. Then check it with Little's law. Twenty permits on a 120 ms call give at most 20 / 0.12 s = 167 calls per second. If payments arrive faster than that, the waiters pile up, and each one waits longer than the last.

Waiting forever is rarely what you want in a payment API. tryAcquire(200, MILLISECONDS) returns false if no permit came in time, so you can answer with a fast 503 or a retry hint instead of a slow timeout. This pattern is usually called a bulkhead, after the walls that stop one flooded section from sinking a ship.

A request that calls two limited downstreams uses two semaphores: take the issuer permit, release it, then take the ledger permit. Don't hold one permit while you wait for another. It ties up the first resource for nothing, and two code paths that take them in opposite orders can deadlock exactly like two locks.

try.title: Shed load instead of queueing forever
steps: ShedLoadDemo sends 1,000 requests at once through a Semaphore(20) guarding a 50 ms call. Each request waits at most 200 ms for a permit.
Predict how many get served. Hint: in 200 ms each permit can serve about 200 / 50 = 4 calls, plus the first round.
Run it, then try -Pargs='20 50 2000' and -Pargs='100 50 200', predicting each first.

code.title: ShedLoadDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** * 1,000 requests arrive at once. The issuer allows 20 calls in flight, each takes 50 ms. * A request waits at most 200 ms for a slot, then gives up (a fast 503 instead of a slow timeout). * * <p>Args: permits, call ms, max wait ms. Default: 20 50 200. */ public class ShedLoadDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { int permits = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 20; long callMs = args.length > 1 ? Long.parseLong(args[1]) : 50; long maxWaitMs = args.length > 2 ? Long.parseLong(args[2]) : 200; Semaphore issuer = new Semaphore(permits); AtomicInteger served = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger shed = new AtomicInteger(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) { perTask.execute(() -> { try { if (!issuer.tryAcquire(maxWaitMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { shed.incrementAndGet(); // no slot in time: fail fast return; } try { Thread.sleep(callMs); // the issuer call served.incrementAndGet(); } finally { issuer.release(); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); } } System.out.printf("permits=%d call=%d ms max wait=%d ms: served %d, shed %d, in %d ms%n", permits, callMs, maxWaitMs, served.get(), shed.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } }

alt.title: ShedLoadDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.vthreads.l03 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** * 1,000 requests arrive at once. The issuer allows 20 calls in flight, each takes 50 ms. * A request waits at most 200 ms for a slot, then gives up (a fast 503 instead of a slow timeout). * * Args: permits, call ms, max wait ms. Default: 20 50 200. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val permits = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 20 val callMs = args.getOrNull(1)?.toLong() ?: 50 val maxWaitMs = args.getOrNull(2)?.toLong() ?: 200 val issuer = Semaphore(permits) val served = AtomicInteger() val shed = AtomicInteger() val t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> repeat(1_000) { perTask.execute { if (!issuer.tryAcquire(maxWaitMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { shed.incrementAndGet() // no slot in time: fail fast return@execute } try { Thread.sleep(callMs) // the issuer call served.incrementAndGet() } finally { issuer.release() } } } } println("permits=%d call=%d ms max wait=%d ms: served %d, shed %d, in %d ms" .format(permits, callMs, maxWaitMs, served.get(), shed.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) }

try.expect: With the defaults, about 100 requests are served (20 permits × 5 rounds; one run here served 94) and the rest are shed in about a third of a second. A 2 s wait serves about 20 × 41 = 820. With 100 permits and 200 ms, about 500 are served. Served requests = permits × (max wait / call time + 1), which is Little's law turned around.

analogy: A semaphore is the stack of visitor badges at a building's front desk. The building (the card issuer) has room for 20 visitors, so there are 20 badges. Visitors who arrive when the stack is empty sit in the lobby, which is cheap, and the next one in line gets a badge when someone hands theirs back on the way out. A pool of 20 virtual threads is like hiring 20 escorts who each walk one visitor through the whole day, the coffee shop included, so visitors who only want coffee wait for an escort too. The analogy breaks at the lobby: a real lobby fills up, but parked virtual threads only cost heap, so the line can grow far longer than you'd want. That is why you set a wait limit.
world: Every downstream in a payment flow has a concurrency contract: the card network's API allows a fixed number of calls in flight per merchant, your Oracle pool has 20 connections, the fraud vendor rate-limits by client. On platform threads the request pool size was hiding those limits. On virtual threads, each one needs its own shared semaphore (or a library bulkhead, such as Resilience4j's, if you already use one) on the client object. In a Kafka consumer that fans out one virtual thread per record in a poll batch, the semaphore is what keeps a 500-record batch from opening 500 calls to the issuer at once.
mistake: The most common mistake is keeping the old habit of a fixed pool and just giving it virtual threads: newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()). It looks like a cheap upgrade and it does limit the database. It also limits every other part of each task, keeps an unbounded queue in front of the pool, and reuses threads, so ThreadLocal state leaks between tasks. The second most common is the opposite: dropping the limit entirely because "virtual threads are cheap", and then sending 5,000 concurrent calls to a downstream that allows 20. Use one virtual thread per task and one shared semaphore per scarce resource.

compare.title: Fan out with a shared limit in Java and Kotlin

java.title: FanOut.java + Bulkhead.java (lab solution, trimmed)
java.html: public final class Bulkhead { private final Semaphore permits; public Bulkhead(int maxConcurrent) { permits = new Semaphore(maxConcurrent); } public <T> T call(Callable<T> work) throws Exception { permits.acquire(); try { return work.call(); } finally { permits.release(); } } } static final Bulkhead ISSUER = new Bulkhead(20); List<String> authorizeAll(List<String> ids) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<String>> fs = new ArrayList<>(); for (String id : ids) fs.add(perTask.submit(() -> ISSUER.call(() -> authorize(id)))); List<String> out = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<String> f : fs) out.add(f.get()); return out; } }

kotlin.title: FanOutKotlin.kt
kotlin.html: package workbench.vthreads.l03 import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore // one limit for the whole service, shared by every caller of the issuer val issuerLimit = Semaphore(20) // acquire, run, always release: the Kotlin version of try/finally around a permit inline fun <T> Semaphore.withPermit(block: () -> T): T { acquire() try { return block() } finally { release() } } fun authorize(id: String): String { Thread.sleep(50) // the blocking issuer call return "auth:$id" } fun authorizeAll(ids: List<String>): List<String> = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> // use {} = try-with-resources ids.map { id -> perTask.submit(Callable { issuerLimit.withPermit { authorize(id) } }) } .map { it.get() } // in input order } fun main() { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val receipts = authorizeAll((1..1_000).map { "pay-$it" }) val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("${receipts.size} receipts, first ${receipts.first()}, last ${receipts.last()}, in $ms ms") }

compare.note: The Kotlin version is the same design: use {} is Kotlin's try-with-resources and works because ExecutorService is AutoCloseable since JDK 19, and an inline extension gives Semaphore a withPermit block. Callable { ... } picks the submit overload that returns a value; a bare lambda can be read as a Runnable. Watch the name clash: kotlinx.coroutines has its own Semaphore with a suspending withPermit, built for coroutines. Inside coroutines use that one, because java.util.concurrent.Semaphore.acquire() blocks the thread. On virtual threads, use the JDK semaphore. Run the Kotlin file with ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l03.FanOutKotlinKt.

worked.title: Send a payout batch to the bank, 20 at a time

steps.say: The bank's payout API allows 20 concurrent calls per client and takes about 150 ms. A batch has 3,000 payouts, and each one also needs an account lookup that has no limit. Start with the limit, as a field on the client that every caller shares.
steps.code: final class BankClient { // one limit for the whole service, from the bank's API contract private final Semaphore inFlight = new Semaphore(20); }

alt.html: class BankClient { // one limit for the whole service, from the bank's API contract private val inFlight = Semaphore(20) }

steps.say: Guard only the bank call. The account lookup happens before acquire(), so 3,000 lookups overlap freely.
steps.code: PayoutResult send(Payout p) throws Exception { Account acct = accounts.lookup(p.accountId()); // 1. unlimited work first inFlight.acquire(); // 2. wait for a slot (parks a virtual thread) try { return bank.payout(acct, p); // 3. the only limited call } finally { inFlight.release(); // 4. always give the slot back } }

alt.html: fun send(p: Payout): PayoutResult { val acct = accounts.lookup(p.accountId) // 1. unlimited work first inFlight.acquire() // 2. wait for a slot (parks a virtual thread) try { return bank.payout(acct, p) // 3. the only limited call } finally { inFlight.release() // 4. always give the slot back } }

steps.say: Fan out one virtual thread per payout, and collect in order. The executor block guarantees that no payout is still running when the method returns.
steps.code: List<PayoutResult> sendAll(List<Payout> batch) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<PayoutResult>> fs = new ArrayList<>(); for (Payout p : batch) fs.add(perTask.submit(() -> send(p))); // 5. fork all List<PayoutResult> results = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<PayoutResult> f : fs) results.add(f.get()); // 6. join in order return results; } }

alt.html: fun sendAll(batch: List<Payout>): List<PayoutResult> = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> val fs = batch.map { p -> perTask.submit(Callable { send(p) }) } // 5. fork all fs.map { it.get() } // 6. join in order }

steps.say: Check the timing with Little's law before you ship it. The bank stage caps you at 20 / 0.15 s = 133 payouts per second, so 3,000 payouts take about 22.5 s no matter how many threads you start. If that is too slow, the fix is a higher limit agreed with the bank, not more threads.

lab.title: Fan out 5,000 calls, never more than 20 in flight
steps: Run the tests once. All six fail.

Write FanOut.callAll: open Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() in try-with-resources, submit one task per input (perTask.submit(() -> call.call(input))), then call get() on each future in order and collect the results.
Write Bulkhead: a Semaphore field built in the constructor, call with acquire() before the try and release() in finally, and available() from availablePermits().

Run the tests. The bulkhead test sends 5,000 calls through Bulkhead(20) and records the most calls that were inside the fake issuer at once. It must be at most 20, and at least 10 to prove the calls overlap.
Read the shared-limit test: two fan-outs run at the same time through one Bulkhead. Think about what would happen if each fan-out made its own.
hints: Inside a lambda, input must be effectively final. The enhanced for loop variable is, so for (I input : inputs) works directly.
Future.get() already throws ExecutionException with the task's exception as the cause, which is exactly what the failure test expects. You don't need to wrap anything.
If the 5,000-call test takes minutes, you are probably waiting on each future right after submitting it. Submit all of them first.

drill.title: The bulkhead from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a class FraudClient whose check(Payment p) method lets at most 50 calls reach http.check(p) at once across the whole service, and gives up with a RejectedExecutionException if no slot frees up within 100 ms. Then compare with the answer: where is acquire relative to the try?

answer.html: final class FraudClient { private final Semaphore inFlight = new Semaphore(50); // shared by every caller private final FraudHttp http; FraudClient(FraudHttp http) { this.http = http; } Risk check(Payment p) throws InterruptedException { if (!inFlight.tryAcquire(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { throw new RejectedExecutionException("fraud service busy"); // fail fast } try { return http.check(p); } finally { inFlight.release(); // only reached if we got a permit } } }

alt.html: class FraudClient(private val http: FraudHttp) { private val inFlight = Semaphore(50) // shared by every caller fun check(p: Payment): Risk { if (!inFlight.tryAcquire(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { throw RejectedExecutionException("fraud service busy") // fail fast } try { return http.check(p) } finally { inFlight.release() // only reached if we got a permit } } }

recap: Start virtual threads with Thread.ofVirtual(), Thread.startVirtualThread, a factory(), or, most often, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().
The per-task executor creates a new, unbounded virtual thread for every task. Open it in try-with-resources: close() waits for every task.
Fork all tasks first, then get() them in order. A failure comes back as an ExecutionException carrying the real cause.
Never pool virtual threads. A pool caps the whole task, keeps a queue, and leaks ThreadLocal state between tasks.
Limit a scarce resource with one shared Semaphore: acquire() before the try, release() in finally, and only around the call that needs it.
Little's law sizes the limit: permits / call time = maximum calls per second. Use tryAcquire with a timeout to shed load instead of queueing forever.

explain.prompt: A teammate proposes Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()) for a batch job "to protect the database, which has 20 connections". Explain why you'd do it differently, and what you'd write instead.
explain.answer: A pool of 20 caps the whole task, not just the database call. Each payout also does lookups and HTTP calls that don't touch the database, and all of that would wait for one of the 20 pool slots too, so the batch runs far slower than it needs to. It also reuses threads, so anything left in a ThreadLocal leaks into the next task. I'd use newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() in a try-with-resources block, one virtual thread per payout, and one shared Semaphore(20) that the database code acquires right around its query, with release() in finally. The database still never sees more than 20 queries, and everything else overlaps freely. Little's law tells us the database stage caps throughput at 20 divided by the query time.

deeper.html:
Concurrency limits and rate limits are different things. A semaphore limits how many calls are in flight. Many APIs instead publish a rate, such as 300 requests per second. Little's law connects the two only if the latency is stable: 20 in flight at 100 ms is 200 per second, but if the API slows to 400 ms, the same 20 permits give 50 per second, while a rate limiter would happily let 300 per second through and pile them up inside the API. If the contract is a rate, use a rate limiter. If it's connections or concurrent calls, use a semaphore. Some teams use both.

Fair or not. new Semaphore(20) is non-fair: a thread that calls acquire() just as a permit is released can take it ahead of threads that have waited longer. That gives better throughput. new Semaphore(20, true) hands permits out in arrival order, which keeps the worst-case wait lower. For a payment API, where a few very slow requests hurt more than a little lost throughput, fair is often the better default.

Very many waiters. Thousands of virtual threads parked on one semaphore are fine. Each release() wakes one waiter, and each waiter costs a parked virtual thread. With hundreds of thousands of waiters, the bigger problem is latency: the last waiter waits for everyone ahead of it. A bounded wait with tryAcquire keeps that under control and turns overload into fast, honest errors.

Structured fan-out. The try-with-resources block guarantees that every thread the method started has finished when it returns. What it doesn't do is stop the other tasks when one fails. Lesson 5 of this track builds that behavior with plain executors, and then shows the JDK's own API for it.
